blocks.text: The examination of the oral cavity and throat is an essential component of general clinical examination, ENT assessment, paediatrics, respiratory medicine and emergency medicine.

It assesses the lips, oral mucosa, gums, teeth, tongue, floor of the mouth, hard and soft palate, uvula, tonsils, oropharynx and posterior pharyngeal wall. It may also include the salivary glands, temporomandibular joint, cervical lymph nodes, voice, swallowing and cranial nerves.
The goal is to identify abnormalities, recognise their clinical significance, detect airway emergencies and present findings clearly to an examiner.
Pen torch
Provides illumination for inspecting the oral cavity, tonsils and posterior pharynx.
Tongue depressors
Help visualise the posterior oral cavity and oropharynx when necessary.
Disposable gloves
Useful when contact with mucosa, saliva, lesions or secretions is anticipated.
Gauze and mouth mirror, if available
Gauze can help hold the tongue when clinically indicated; a mouth mirror can help inspect teeth and oral surfaces.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity and explain the examination.
Obtain consent and position the patient sitting upright.
Ask about oral pain, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, voice changes and dental problems.
Ensure adequate lighting and use a tongue depressor when necessary.
Wear gloves if contact with the oral mucosa or secretions is expected.
Ask about dentures, oral appliances, recent dental procedures and relevant allergies if applicable.

blocks.text: Safety first: If the patient has stridor, respiratory distress, drooling with inability to swallow, rapidly progressive tongue or neck swelling, or a suspected deep neck infection, assess the airway and obtain emergency assistance. Do not force the mouth open or repeatedly manipulate the throat in a patient with suspected airway compromise.

subsections.subsection_title: 2. General inspection before examining individual structures

blocks.text: Begin by observing the patient before asking them to open their mouth.

items.text: Drooling or inability to handle secretions.
Difficulty speaking or a muffled voice.
Trismus, meaning difficulty opening the mouth.
Dehydration, such as dry mucous membranes.
Muffled “hot-potato” voice, trismus and unilateral throat swelling may indicate a peritonsillar abscess.
Drooling, dysphagia, stridor and respiratory distress may indicate a serious airway or deep neck emergency.
Hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks, especially with smoking history, a neck mass or progressive symptoms, warrants appropriate ENT assessment.
Trismus can result from dental infection, peritonsillar infection, temporomandibular joint disease or other pathology.

blocks.text: Inspect the upper and lower lips, the vermilion border, corners of the mouth and visible inner lip mucosa.
Angular cheilitis
Inflammation and fissuring at the corners of the mouth. Possible contributors include saliva irritation, Candida or bacterial infection, nutritional deficiencies and poorly fitting dentures.
Herpes labialis
Grouped vesicles or crusted lesions, commonly around the vermilion border. Often preceded by tingling or burning.
Persistent lip or mucosal lesion
An unexplained ulcer, indurated lesion, or persistent white or red patch requires assessment, especially if it does not heal within approximately two to three weeks.

items.text: Dry, cracked lips may occur with dehydration, environmental exposure or lip licking.
Pallor may accompany anaemia but should be assessed alongside other clinical findings.
Central or peripheral cyanosis requires interpretation in the context of oxygenation and circulation.
Persistent induration, bleeding, an enlarging lesion or a non-healing ulcer raises concern for malignancy.

blocks.text: OSCE tip: Do not inspect only the external lips. Evert them gently when appropriate to examine the inner mucosal surfaces.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Examination of the oral mucosa and buccal cavity

blocks.text: The oral mucosa lines the inside of the cheeks and lips. Inspect it before concentrating on the teeth and tongue.

items.text: Ask the patient to open their mouth.
Use the pen torch to illuminate the oral cavity.
Inspect the inner surface of the upper and lower lips.
Ask the patient to open their cheeks gently, using a tongue depressor if needed.
Look for lesions, patches, ulcers, pigmentation and swelling.
Inspect the opening of the parotid duct opposite the upper second molar on each side.

blocks.text: Oral candidiasis (thrush)

White plaques that can often be wiped away, leaving an erythematous surface. It is associated with factors such as recent antibiotics, inhaled corticosteroids, immunosuppression and diabetes. Not every white oral lesion is candidiasis.
Leukoplakia
A predominantly white plaque that cannot be classified as another specific disorder. Persistent unexplained white patches require assessment because some lesions have premalignant potential.
Erythroplakia
A persistent red patch that cannot readily be attributed to another condition. It warrants prompt specialist assessment because of its association with oral epithelial dysplasia and malignancy.
Aphthous ulceration
Typically presents as a painful, shallow ulcer with a pale or yellowish centre and an erythematous border. Recurrent, unusually large, persistent or multiple ulcers may warrant further investigation.

Clinical pearl: A persistent oral ulcer, red or white patch, unexplained lump or indurated lesion—particularly in someone who uses tobacco, areca nut or heavy alcohol—should not be dismissed as simple infection.
Dental disease is an important cause of oral pain, facial swelling, referred ear pain and difficulty eating.
Ask the patient to open their mouth widely. Inspect the upper and lower dental arches systematically.

items.text: Number of teeth and missing teeth.
Loose or displaced teeth, if apparent.
Dentures, crowns and other dental appliances.

blocks.text: Ask the patient to bite together gently if you need to assess the bite.

content_groups.group_title: B. Common findings and their significance

rows: Dental caries
Tooth decay, which may progress to pulpitis or dental abscess
Broken or fractured tooth
May cause pain, infection or trauma to adjacent tissues
Missing teeth
Previous extraction, trauma or dental disease
Plaque and calculus
Increased risk of gingivitis and periodontal disease
Malocclusion
May affect chewing and, in some cases, contribute to functional problems
Dental abscess
May cause severe pain, local swelling, fever and spreading infection

blocks.text: Inspect the gingiva around the teeth.

items.text: Periodontal pockets, if you are equipped and trained to assess them.

blocks.text: Gingivitis causes inflammation of the gingiva and may produce bleeding with brushing. Periodontitis involves destruction of the supporting structures of the teeth and can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss.

blocks.title: A dental abscess may present with:

items.text: Swelling of the gum or face.
Fever or systemic illness in more severe cases.

blocks.text: Facial swelling accompanied by floor-of-mouth swelling, tongue elevation, drooling, dysphagia or breathing difficulty may indicate a spreading infection such as Ludwig angina. This is an emergency.

OSCE tip: Inspect the teeth and gums even when the main complaint is sore throat or ear pain. Dental pathology can produce referred pain, and a normal-looking pharynx does not exclude an odontogenic cause.
The tongue should be examined systematically on its dorsal surface, lateral borders, tip, underside and mobility.
Ask the patient to protrude the tongue.
A normal tongue is generally moist, pink and mobile, with visible papillae. Its appearance varies with hydration, diet and individual anatomy.

content_groups.group_title: B. Inspect the lateral borders and underside

blocks.text: Ask the patient to move the tongue from side to side. If necessary, ask them to lift the tongue towards the roof of the mouth.
For a more complete examination, gently hold the tip of the tongue with gauze, using appropriate infection-control precautions, and inspect the lateral borders and ventral surface.
The lateral and ventral tongue are important sites to inspect for suspicious lesions. A persistent ulcer or indurated lesion in these areas requires prompt assessment.

items.text: Move it to the left and right.
Push it against the inside of each cheek.

blocks.text: Observe for weakness, restricted movement, tremor, fasciculations or deviation.

Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII): A lower motor neuron lesion may cause the protruded tongue to deviate towards the side of the lesion, often with wasting and fasciculations. An upper motor neuron lesion may cause deviation away from the cerebral lesion, although the pattern depends on the site of injury.
Glossitis
Inflammation of the tongue, sometimes producing redness, tenderness or a smooth surface. Possible causes include nutritional deficiencies, infection, irritation and systemic disease.
Geographic tongue
Irregular erythematous patches with pale or white borders that may change location over time. Usually benign, although some patients experience sensitivity.
Oral candidiasis
White plaques or erythematous changes, sometimes with soreness or altered taste. The diagnosis depends on the appearance and clinical context.
Suspicious tongue lesion
A persistent ulcer, induration, unexplained red or white patch, or mass requires prompt assessment, particularly on the lateral tongue or floor of the mouth.

content_groups.group_title: E. The floor of the mouth

blocks.text: Ask the patient to lift the tongue and inspect the floor of the mouth.

Bilateral, firm swelling of the floor of the mouth with tongue elevation may indicate Ludwig angina, a potentially life-threatening deep neck infection. It requires emergency airway and hospital assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. Examination of the hard palate and soft palate

blocks.text: The palate separates the oral cavity from the nasal cavity and plays an important role in speech and swallowing.
The hard palate is the anterior bony portion of the roof of the mouth.
Procedure
Ask the patient to open their mouth and tilt their head slightly backwards if comfortable. Illuminate the roof of the mouth.

items.text: Cleft palate or other congenital abnormalities.

blocks.text: A normal hard palate is generally pink, although its appearance varies with pigmentation and local factors.
A midline bony prominence may represent a benign torus palatinus. An unexplained ulcer, persistent lump or destructive lesion requires further assessment.
The soft palate is the posterior muscular portion of the roof of the mouth.
Ask the patient to open their mouth and say “ah.”

items.text: Movement relative to the pharyngeal walls.

blocks.text: Normal elevation is generally symmetrical.
The soft palate helps separate the nasopharynx from the oropharynx during swallowing and contributes to speech resonance.

items.text: Unilateral palatal weakness may occur with vagal pathway dysfunction.
Nasal regurgitation of liquids can suggest impaired palatal closure.
A bifid uvula may be associated with a submucous cleft palate in some patients.
Palatal petechiae may occur in streptococcal pharyngitis and other conditions, but are not diagnostic on their own.

blocks.text: The uvula is the small midline projection hanging from the posterior edge of the soft palate.

items.text: Ask the patient to open their mouth.
Observe the uvula's position and movement.
Assess whether the soft palate rises symmetrically.
Look for swelling, ulceration, erythema or displacement.

blocks.text: The uvula is centrally positioned and moves with the soft palate during phonation.
Uvula deviation

Deviation away from a unilateral peritonsillar abscess can occur because swelling displaces the uvula towards the opposite side. However, uvular deviation alone is not sufficient to diagnose an abscess.
Deviation may also result from palatal weakness or other structural abnormalities.
Uvulitis
Inflammation causes swelling, erythema and sometimes pain or a foreign-body sensation. Severe swelling associated with breathing difficulty requires emergency assessment.
Bifid uvula
A split or forked uvula may be a normal variant but can be associated with a submucous cleft palate.

Routine elicitation is not necessary in every oral examination. When clinically indicated, assess the reflex carefully in an appropriate setting. Palatal movement, voice quality and swallowing provide additional information about bulbar function.
An absent gag reflex alone does not establish a neurological lesion, because the reflex may be absent in healthy individuals.
The palatine tonsils lie between the anterior and posterior tonsillar pillars on either side of the oropharynx.

items.text: Ask the patient to open their mouth widely.
Shine the pen torch into the oropharynx.
If the tonsils are difficult to visualise, use a tongue depressor to depress the anterior tongue gently.
Inspect both tonsils and compare their size.
Examine the anterior and posterior pillars.
Assess colour, surface, exudate, ulceration and surrounding swelling.
Observe the position of the uvula.
Assess for trismus, drooling, voice changes or respiratory difficulty.

blocks.text: Avoid pressing deeply on the tongue or repeatedly stimulating the posterior pharynx, as this can provoke gagging or vomiting.
The commonly used Brodsky scale grades the tonsils according to how much of the oropharyngeal width they occupy.

rows: Tonsils absent or within the tonsillar fossa
Occupy less than 25% of the oropharyngeal width
Occupy approximately 25–50%
Occupy approximately 50–75%
Occupy approximately 75% or more; may nearly touch or meet at the midline

blocks.text: Grading is approximate and depends on the examination technique and anatomy. Tonsil size alone does not establish the severity of infection or the presence of obstructive sleep apnoea.
Acute tonsillitis
Enlarged, erythematous tonsils, sometimes with white or yellow exudate. Causes include viral and bacterial infections. Exudate alone does not prove a bacterial cause.
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)

Often causes severe unilateral throat pain, trismus, a muffled voice, unilateral palatal or peritonsillar swelling and displacement of the uvula away from the affected side. Requires urgent assessment.
Tonsillolith
White or yellow material within tonsillar crypts. It may cause halitosis, a foreign-body sensation or discomfort and is not necessarily acute infection.

blocks.title: Persistent or unexplained unilateral enlargement deserves assessment, particularly when associated with:

blocks.text: These findings do not automatically mean malignancy, but they should not be ignored.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Examination of the oropharynx and posterior pharyngeal wall

blocks.text: The oropharynx includes the region behind the oral cavity, including the tonsils, tonsillar pillars, soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall.

items.text: Ask the patient to open their mouth widely.
Ask them to say “ah” to assess palatal movement.
Use a tongue depressor gently if the tongue obscures the view.
Inspect the posterior pharyngeal wall, tonsillar pillars and surrounding mucosa.
Look for erythema, exudate, ulcers, swelling, asymmetry, postnasal secretions or masses.
Observe for pooling of secretions or difficulty handling saliva.

blocks.text: Pharyngitis

Inflammation of the pharynx can cause erythema, pain and discomfort on swallowing. Viral causes are common, but bacterial infection is also possible. Appearance alone is insufficient to determine the cause.
Posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning
A bumpy appearance may be associated with chronic irritation, including postnasal drainage or allergic rhinitis. It is not diagnostic on its own.
Exudate

White or yellow material can occur in several conditions, including streptococcal infection, infectious mononucleosis and other infections. Clinical features and appropriate testing guide the diagnosis.
Asymmetrical swelling or a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall
May indicate a deep neck infection, such as a retropharyngeal abscess, particularly in a child with fever, neck stiffness, drooling or difficulty swallowing. This requires urgent assessment.

Important safety point: If epiglottitis or a significant deep neck infection is suspected, avoid forceful tongue depression or attempts to inspect deeply into the throat. Urgent airway-capable assessment is more important than completing the routine examination.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Assessment of the floor of the mouth and salivary glands

blocks.text: These structures are sometimes omitted from routine OSCEs but are important when assessing oral pain, swelling, dry mouth or difficulty swallowing.
Ask the patient to raise their tongue.
The submandibular ducts (Wharton's ducts) open on either side of the lingual frenulum.
Inspect and palpate the parotid and submandibular regions if indicated.

items.text: Dry mouth or reduced salivary flow.

blocks.text: Swelling and pain around meals may suggest salivary duct obstruction. Fever, tenderness and purulent discharge may indicate infection.
This is a rapidly progressive infection of the floor of the mouth and submandibular spaces, often arising from a dental source.
It is a life-threatening airway emergency. Do not delay emergency treatment to complete the oral examination.
The oral cavity and oropharynx drain into cervical lymph node groups. Examination of the neck is therefore an important extension of the throat examination.

items.text: Explain that you will examine the neck and obtain consent.
Position the patient comfortably, with the neck slightly flexed.
Inspect for visible swelling or asymmetry.
Assess any enlarged nodes for tenderness, size, consistency, mobility and matting.
Examine the supraclavicular regions when indicated.
Deep cervical chain, using appropriate technique.

rows: Tender, mobile nodes during an acute sore throat
Often reactive to infection
Enlarged tonsillar or jugulodigastric nodes
May accompany tonsillitis or other oropharyngeal inflammation
Persistent hard or fixed cervical node
Requires assessment for malignancy or other significant pathology
Generalised lymphadenopathy
May occur in systemic infections, haematological disorders and other diseases
Cervical node with a persistent oral lesion
Requires investigation for possible oral or oropharyngeal malignancy

blocks.text: Node characteristics alone cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant disease. Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy, especially with a neck mass, dysphagia, hoarseness or weight loss, warrants further assessment.
These are functional components of the throat examination and can reveal abnormalities not apparent from inspection alone.

blocks.title: Ask the patient to speak in a normal voice and listen for:

blocks.text: Clinical interpretation

items.text: Hoarseness may result from laryngitis, vocal cord pathology or recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction.
Hypernasal speech may occur when the soft palate does not close adequately against the pharynx.
A muffled voice with trismus and unilateral throat swelling may suggest a peritonsillar abscess.
Stridor suggests upper airway narrowing and may represent an emergency.

blocks.text: Ask whether the patient has difficulty swallowing food, liquids or saliva.

items.text: Globus sensation: a sensation of a lump in the throat, often without actual obstruction.
Nasal regurgitation: liquids or food passing into the nose, which may indicate impaired palatal closure.

blocks.text: Ask about coughing or choking while swallowing, recurrent chest infections, food sticking, progressive symptoms and weight loss.
A patient who cannot swallow their saliva, is drooling, or has respiratory distress requires urgent assessment.

content_groups.group_title: C. Cranial nerves relevant to the throat

rows: CN V — Trigeminal
Facial sensation, jaw movement and mastication when indicated
CN VII — Facial
Facial symmetry and movements
CN IX — Glossopharyngeal
Relevant pharyngeal sensation and afferent component of the gag reflex
CN X — Vagus
Palatal movement, voice, swallowing and efferent component of the gag reflex
CN XII — Hypoglossal
Tongue movement, deviation, wasting and fasciculations

blocks.text: A focused neurological assessment is especially important if the patient has dysphagia, dysarthria, palatal asymmetry, tongue deviation or other neurological symptoms.
Not every patient requires these investigations. Select them according to the history and examination findings.

content_groups.group_title: A. Throat swab or rapid antigen testing

blocks.text: When streptococcal pharyngitis is suspected, appropriate testing may include a rapid antigen detection test or throat culture, depending on age, local guidance and availability.
Tonsillar exudate alone does not confirm streptococcal infection. Clinical features, validated decision rules and testing guide management.
A trained clinician may use a flexible endoscope to examine the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, pharynx and larynx when symptoms suggest pathology beyond the visible oral cavity.
It may be indicated for persistent hoarseness, suspected nasopharyngeal disease, unexplained unilateral middle-ear effusion, or selected swallowing and airway symptoms.

blocks.title: Imaging may be indicated when there is concern for:

items.text: An abscess extending beyond the visible tissues.

blocks.text: Contrast-enhanced CT is commonly used to evaluate suspected deep neck infection in a stable patient when imaging is indicated. Airway management and specialist assessment take priority if the patient is unstable.
A biopsy may be required for a suspicious or persistent oral lesion, especially if there is induration, ulceration, an unexplained red or white patch, or a mass.
Do not assume a persistent lesion is benign solely because it is painless.
Acute tonsillitis or pharyngitis
Sore throat, painful swallowing, erythematous pharynx and possibly enlarged tonsils or exudate. Viral and bacterial causes must be distinguished clinically and, when indicated, by testing.
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
Severe unilateral throat pain, trismus, muffled voice, peritonsillar swelling and possible uvular deviation. Requires urgent assessment.
Oral candidiasis
White plaques or erythematous mucosal changes, sometimes with soreness or altered taste. Assess risk factors and distinguish it from other white lesions.
Ludwig angina
Rapidly progressive floor-of-mouth and submandibular swelling, often from dental infection. Tongue elevation, drooling or breathing difficulty indicate an emergency.
Possible oral malignancy
A persistent ulcer, indurated lesion, unexplained red or white patch, or neck mass requires prompt assessment and potentially biopsy.

items.text: Examining the tonsils but forgetting the lips, buccal mucosa, gums and teeth.
Failing to inspect the lateral and ventral surfaces of the tongue.
Missing lesions on the floor of the mouth.
Using the tongue depressor too forcefully or provoking excessive gagging.
Recording tonsillar exudate as proof of bacterial infection.
Ignoring the soft palate and uvula while asking the patient to say “ah.”
Failing to assess voice, swallowing or airway symptoms.
Manipulating the throat when a deep neck infection or airway emergency is suspected.
Documenting normal findings in areas that were not adequately visualised.

subsections.subsection_title: 17. How to present your findings to the examiner

blocks.text: A good presentation should follow the anatomical sequence and include the important positive and negative findings.
**Oral Cavity and Throat Examination — Sample Normal Findings**

The lips were symmetrical, with no ulceration, swelling or fissuring. The oral mucosa was moist, with no obvious ulcers, white plaques or suspicious lesions. The teeth and gingiva showed no obvious caries, significant inflammation or swelling.
The tongue was pink and moist, with no obvious coating, ulceration or mass. It protruded in the midline, with normal movement. The floor of the mouth was unremarkable.
The hard and soft palates were intact, with no obvious lesions. The soft palate elevated symmetrically on phonation, and the uvula remained centrally positioned.
The tonsils were symmetrical, with no significant enlargement, erythema or exudate. The posterior pharyngeal wall showed no obvious erythema, swelling or exudate.
There was no obvious cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient's voice was clear, with no obvious hoarseness or muffled quality.
**Conclusion:** No obvious abnormality was identified in the components of the oral cavity and throat examination performed.
Only report findings that you have actually assessed. If you could not adequately visualise the posterior pharynx or inspect the floor of the mouth, state this limitation.
Use this checklist to practise the examination in a consistent order.
0 of 17
Introduce yourself, obtain consent and assess airway warning signs
Inspect the face, lips and corners of the mouth
Inspect inner lips and buccal mucosa
Inspect teeth, gums and dental arches
Inspect dorsal, lateral and ventral surfaces of the tongue
Assess tongue protrusion and movement
Inspect the floor of the mouth and salivary duct openings
Inspect the hard palate
Ask the patient to say 'ah' and assess soft palate movement
Inspect the uvula for position, symmetry and lesions
Inspect both tonsils, tonsillar pillars and surrounding tissues
Inspect the posterior pharyngeal wall
Assess voice, speech and swallowing symptoms
Palpate relevant cervical lymph node groups
Assess cranial nerves when indicated
Identify suspicious lesions and urgent airway or infection warning signs
Present findings clearly and state any limitations

items.text: CN IX: afferent limb of the gag reflex.
CN X: efferent limb of the gag reflex; also important for palatal movement, voice and swallowing.
CN XII: controls tongue movement; a lower motor neuron lesion may cause ipsilateral deviation, wasting and fasciculations.
Uvula deviation away from a unilateral swelling: consider a peritonsillar abscess in the appropriate clinical context.
Trismus, unilateral throat swelling and a muffled voice: suspect quinsy or another deep infection.
White oral plaques: consider candidiasis, but exclude other mucosal disorders.
Persistent oral ulcer or suspicious red or white patch: requires assessment rather than repeated empirical treatment.
Tongue elevation with floor-of-mouth swelling: consider Ludwig angina.
Drooling, stridor or inability to swallow secretions: prioritise emergency airway assessment.

blocks.text: The key to a high-scoring OSCE is to examine systematically, understand the significance of each abnormality, extend the examination when clinically indicated, and recognise when an apparently routine sore throat may represent a serious airway or deep neck infection.
